Neurology · published research

Perioperative neurocognitive disorder (PND)

Four aged-mouse publications report better learning or memory and changes in synaptic, inflammatory or myelin-related markers after PBM. No human treatment study was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Four aged-mouse publications report better learning or memory and changes in synaptic, inflammatory or myelin-related markers after PBM. No human treatment study was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

The mapped perioperative neurocognitive disorder and postoperative neurocognitive disorder categories contain four unique publications. All are animal studies in aged mice. The papers test different proposed pathways, including mitochondrial function, remyelination, IRF7 and SIRT3-related signaling. They are distinct publication reports, but repeated surgical models and related research groups mean that the total does not establish four independent clinical replications.

Human and clinical evidence

No human treatment trial or patient cohort was identified for PBM in perioperative neurocognitive disorder. The evidence does not address cognition after surgery in older people.

Animal evidence

The four mouse studies report improvement in learning or memory tests after surgery or anesthesia, alongside changes in synaptic proteins, oxidative stress, neuroinflammatory markers or myelin-related pathways. One aged-mouse study reported better cognitive performance and increased synaptic markers after near-infrared treatment (Zhong et al. 2023). Another found improved learning and memory measures with changes in IRF7 expression and microglial phenotype (Zhang et al. 2024). The outcomes are animal behavior and molecular markers rather than postoperative patient function.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified. Cellular and inflammatory markers were measured in mouse brain tissue within the animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The studies generally use transcranial near-infrared light, including a reported 810-nm protocol. They differ in surgery model, treatment timing, session schedule and measured pathway. Complete matching dose data are not available across all four papers. A transcranial mouse procedure cannot be assumed to deliver the same brain dose or effect in older patients.

Interpretation

These studies support further testing of PBM in postoperative mouse models and identify several measurable pathways. They do not show that PBM prevents delirium or postoperative cognitive decline in people. The main uncertainty is the absence of direct human outcomes and the limited independent replication across clinically relevant settings.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for preventing perioperative neurocognitive disorder in people because the evidence is limited to aged-mouse models. Low within those models for selected learning, memory and tissue-marker outcomes.
Publications and records4 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Four mouse publications report improved cognitive or tissue outcomes after surgery-related injury, but no human trial or independent clinical cohort is available. The studies use related aged-mouse models and different proposed pathways. Human research should test safety and feasibility first, then evaluate cognition and daily function against sham with adequate follow-up.
